NewGen are HIRING 📢 And it’s for two roles that are *completely* new to our industry…

We’re looking for: a Head of Clipping and a Clipping Specialist.

It’s no secret that short form has made clipping HUGE. Half the internet is now someone else’s video cut into 20 second clips.

We know there’s a massive future in this kind of content, so we’re building the infrastructure into NewGen right now.

Head of Clipping is the big one. You’ll be building the proposition from scratch, owning the clipper network and the commercial model, and shaping the tech inside our AI tool, NewGen Multiple. We're hiring: Robotics Engineer, navigation & onboard compute for a robot dog 🤖
Dubai / Abu Dhabi · on-site with the robot · start now

At Zurbagun Robotics we give every robot a profession. We take off-the-shelf robots and write the software that lets them do new jobs.

Where we are:
Our Unitree Go2 Pro already takes orders from an AI agent. Say "find the iron and go to it", and the agent looks through the camera and tells the dog what to do. Right now it all runs on a laptop over Wi-Fi, and the dog has no map. That's what you'll fix.

Your first 2–3 weeks (paid trial sprint):
→ Lidar mapping, localization and collision-free navigation (Nav2 or your stack of choice)
→ Skills the agent can call: go to an object, follow a route, return to base, follow a person. The agent decides, the skill executes on its own
→ A Jetson in a backpack on the dog: power, mounting, and moving everything off the laptop
→ Demo day: you tell the dog to find something and it walks there using the map. Live.

What's next:
The dog walks construction sites daily with a lidar and a 360 camera, so we can check what's built against the BIM model and inspect apartments before handover. Then a second dog, several robots at once, outdoor work in Gulf heat, and more robots on the same software.

You:
- Hands-on experience with robot dogs, humanoids or other mobile robots, controlled from code
- Python, ROS2, Nav2 / Cartographer / RTAB-Map or similar
- Linux and Jetson (or similar embedded compute)
- Bonus: lidar & point clouds, Isaac Sim / MuJoCo, LLM agents, speech recognition
- Able to be with the robot in Dubai or Abu Dhabi at least 2–3 days a week

We offer:
- A paid sprint, hourly or fixed fee, and you name the rate. Then full-time or contract, your call
- Robot, workspace and all hardware on us
- A small team with a direct line to the founders and no layers of approval
- A rare chance to take AI agents out of the chat window and into the physical world

To apply, DM me here, message me on Telegram @nikizlyfe, or email nik@zurbagun.ai with:
· the robots you've worked with and what you've done on navigation
· GitHub or a video
· your CV or LinkedIn

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) plans to ensure that around 80% of its future new hires have digital and artificial intelligence skills, as the IT services company expands its AI business and looks to improve profitability. Chief Operating Officer Arathi Subramanian  shared the hiring outlook in an interview with PTI.

The company added 4,500 employees in the September quarter, of whom 25% to 30% had specialised AI skills, while around 80% had what Subramanian described as “new-age” skills. She said TCS expects this hiring mix to continue, adding that the required talent is available in the market.

AI-led work accounted for 10% of TCS’ revenue in the quarter ended September 2026. Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director K Krithivasan said a growing contribution from AI projects could support margin expansion as these engagements increase in volume.

TCS is also continuing to invest in specialised talent, partnerships and acquisitions. Krithivasan said professionals willing to learn new skills can benefit from their existing understanding of technology and industry domains, suggesting that AI-driven changes in the workforce will not necessarily favour fresh graduates over experienced engineers.

The company said customers are often starting with AI projects in specific business areas before expanding them after seeing results. While TCS is cautious about classifying deals as AI-led, Krithivasan said some element of AI is now involved in virtually all the company’s work. Its second-quarter total contract value stood at $9.6 billion.

The strategy comes as IT services companies face pressure to adapt their delivery models to AI, which can improve productivity but also challenge traditional billing models. TCS reported an operating margin of 24% for the September quarter and annualised AI revenue of $3.1 billion.

Procurement Professionals over 40 years of age are Facing difficulties in landing new jobs, here is why:

Procurement Professionals can inbox their CV for a Free Review And Feedback.

1. Age and Salary Expectation Bias: Some employers may hesitate to recruit experienced procurement professionals due to assumptions about salary expectations, adaptability, or willingness to work in positions with narrower purchasing responsibilities.

2. AI and Automation Adaptability Bias: Some employers assume experienced procurement professionals may struggle to adapt to e-procurement platforms, AI-powered sourcing tools, automated purchasing workflows, and emerging supply chain technologies, overlooking their actual capabilities.

3. Unfamiliarity with Modern CV Requirements: After years in procurement, you may not know what today's HR professionals and hiring managers expect to see in a CV, how they assess candidates, or which procurement achievements deserve priority.

4. Overemphasis on Older Experience: Focus on your most recent 10 years. Summarise earlier positions instead of detailing every purchasing responsibility, keeping attention on your current procurement capabilities and strategic sourcing experience.

5. Responsibilities Instead of Achievements: Listing routine purchase orders, supplier coordination, and quotation comparisons without demonstrating cost savings, supplier performance improvements, procurement efficiency, or contract value optimisation weakens your profile.

6. Limited Procurement Software Visibility: Employers may look for proficiency in SAP Ariba, Oracle Procurement, Coupa, Microsoft Dynamics, ERP systems, or other role-specific sourcing platforms. Your CV must reflect the tools you genuinely use.

7. Changing Procurement and Compliance Requirements: Updated procurement policies, supplier due diligence requirements, contract regulations, sustainability standards, and public or private sector compliance frameworks can influence hiring decisions.

8. Weak Analytical and Digital Skills: Limited evidence of expertise in spend analysis, demand forecasting, supplier risk assessment, advanced Excel, procurement dashboards, or automated purchasing reports may affect competitiveness for certain roles.

Could the Dutch freelance market finally be getting some clarity? 

The Netherlands has just opened consultation on its proposed Zelfstandigenwet (Self-Employed Persons Act).

And for anyone involved in freelance or contract hiring, this could be a big development.

Over the past couple of years, uncertainty around Wet DBA and false self-employment has made many businesses increasingly cautious about engaging freelancers.

Even when they genuinely need specialist expertise.

The proposed legislation aims to change that by introducing clearer criteria around:

→ Whether someone is genuinely operating as an independent business.
→ How much freedom they have over delivering their work.
→ Whether they carry their own commercial risks.

The idea is to give businesses and freelancers greater certainty before an assignment even begins. And from a Data amp; AI recruitment perspective, that's particularly interesting.

Businesses still need specialist engineers, architects and AI professionals to deliver complex transformation projects, often for defined periods rather than permanent headcount.

But uncertainty around contractor engagement can make accessing that expertise more complicated. Of course, its still only a proposal, with implementation targeted for 2028.

The real question is whether clearer legislation would actually encourage businesses to start engaging freelancers more confidently again.

Or whether budgets, internal hiring policies and project approvals are now the bigger barriers. Interested to hear from hiring managers and freelancers across the Netherlands.

Would the Zelfstandigenwet change your approach to contract hiring?

In the past couple of weeks, I have been fielding the same nervous, rigid question from bright master’s students, PhD researchers, and young professionals:

*“Are you using AI? Is it even allowed in your organization?”*

The anxiety behind the question is palpable. And it reveals just how completely academia is preparing another generation to be unprepared.

Right now, our app studio is shifting accessibility from an afterthought into the core inception phase of digital products. Our communications agency fuses accessibility with narrative strategy. With my co-founder, we are building accessible infrastructure for sports. This week, I am signing a contract with UNICEF Bulgaria on how climate change impacts children and young people with disabilities, alongside kicking off other major initiatives.

When your work directly impacts real human beings, your primary currency is **delivery**, not academic purity.

Yet public discourse remains trapped in a laughable, bipartisan theater:

On one side, ideological self-sabotage treats computational leverage as an existential betrayal of the human soul. No, I do not care if a 5,000-word piece of critical research is structured, edited, and accelerated using tools trained on human knowledge—as long as the voice, ethics, and direction are mine, and the output serves the vulnerable communities counting on it.

On the other side, market smugness insists that true sophistication means hiring layers of expensive consultants to do what a focused prompt and a direct execution engine can achieve in seconds. That isn’t strategic depth; it is institutional inertia disguised as prestige.

To the students and early-career researchers currently frozen by institutional panic: 

Your universities are teaching you to obsess over the tool instead of the problem. A hammer does not possess ethics, vision, or empathy—you do. The tool doesn't think; it executes. What matters is the critical mind directing it, the lived experience informing it, and the courage to build something that actually functions in the physical world.

Real-world impact is not a multiple-choice exam. Step out of the ideological binary, use the best instruments available, and start building.

When I look back at H1, six hiring assignments at Corenza come to mind.

Each company had a different requirement, and honestly, each one needed a different approach.

Here’s what we worked on.

- A telecom company needed people quickly. We closed 3 IDT contract staffing roles within a month.

- A GCC was expanding its India operations. We closed 13 AI Analyst roles.

- A global AI music company needed a Finance Head for its GCC. We closed the mandate.

- A FinTech preparing for an IPO needed people across Financial Reporting and Internal Audit.

- A pharma company needed a new CFO before the existing one left. We helped complete the appointment in time for knowledge transfer.

- A CleanTech company was looking for a VP – Finance. Through targeted talent mapping, we hired a senior Finance leader from the energy sector.

Six different assignments, and each had its own challenges.

Some needed quick closures. Some needed very specific talent. And some needed the right person at the right time.

That's one thing I've learned as a founder: recruitment is not just about filling a position. 

You need to understand why the company is hiring and what it expects from that person.
That's what we try to get right at Corenza.

The same specialist can cost 3–10 times more depending on the country. So why are companies still limiting their talent searches to one market?

BricsProf has released its BRICS Talent Barometer for Q2 2026, exploring cross-border hiring trends, talent shortages and opportunities across BRICS countries, including the UAE.

A few findings I found particularly interesting:

1. Cross-border hiring is already happening at scale.

Around 5,000 Russian IT specialists were hired by foreign companies, primarily Chinese, in 2024 — twice as many as the previous year.

Demand for Russian professionals in the UAE reportedly increased by 117% year-on-year, particularly in IT, finance and compliance.

2. Talent shortages in one country often match talent availability in another.

According to the report:

• India has a strong supply of mid-level developers, QA specialists and engineers.

• South Africa and India offer English-speaking customer support, sales and back-office professionals.

• Russia has experienced senior IT architects and project managers in demand across China, the UAE and India.

• AI, data and cybersecurity specialists remain in short supply across all five major BRICS markets.

3. Cost differences create opportunities for employers.

The report estimates that companies can potentially hire remote specialists at 30–70% below local costs, depending on the profession and country.

But the opportunity is not just about reducing costs. It is also about accessing expertise, entering new markets and building teams across time zones.

4. AI is changing what companies hire for.

Upwork reported 40% year-on-year growth in AI-related work in Q1 2026, while traditional freelance categories faced pressure.

The demand is shifting towards verified specialists, experienced professionals and teams capable of delivering measurable results.

5. Cross-border hiring is becoming more regulated.

China, India, Russia, Brazil and South Africa are introducing or considering changes to platform employment regulations.

For companies, finding international talent is only part of the challenge. Structuring contracts, payments and compliance correctly is becoming equally important.

My takeaway for employers in the UAE and GCC:

Remote hiring is not necessarily the answer for every position. But for IT, engineering, business development, specialised projects and certain back-office functions, expanding the search beyond the local market can create a real competitive advantage.

And with the right infrastructure, language barriers, contracts and international payments become much easier to manage.

Founders quite often hire their first sales leader to stop selling.

That is usually where it starts to go wrong.

SaaStr Ai spent last week publishing posts on hiring, and firing, VPs of Sales. The core advice is simple. Hire only after the founder has proven the sale. Look for someone who has already done your next stage, at your deal size. And be careful with big-company candidates, because they often expect resources you don't have.

In Central Europe I see the same story with a local twist.

The owner built the company on personal relationships. Then he hires a manager with a strong corporate logo on the CV and expects the system to arrive with him. The manager expects the system to be there already. Six months later both are disappointed, and the owner still holds the key accounts (and the final word on every discount).

I have been on both sides of this. Eleven years at 3M, where the amazing system existed before I did, and then growing companies, where we built it while selling.

What I see most often: the owner waits for this hire like for a saviour. Yet nobody has written down what success should look like, who the ideal customer is, or any proof that the sale works without the owner in the room.

Founders/CEOs/Decision makers: Before you sign that contract, answer four questions honestly:
→ What exactly should be different in 90 days, in numbers?
→ Who is your customer, in one sentence your team can repeat?
→ Where is the proof that someone other than you has closed a deal?
→ Who decides on price after day one?

If you can't answer them, you are hiring hope with a corporate CV.

Most of my work involves speaking with HR managers in IT companies about staffing.

One clear gap I keep hearing: HR managers struggle to find candidates for contract roles, while most qualified candidates still prefer full-time jobs.

I get it — full-time brings stability, benefits, and certainty.

But here’s what’s changing in the industry:
• AI is shrinking project timelines. A 2-year project is now often done in 6–9 months, making full-time hiring riskier for companies.

• Clients now prefer fixed project costs over hourly rates, squeezing IT companies’ margins.

• Offshore work is declining. US and European clients now prefer nearshore partners in similar time zones, so companies can’t keep people on the bench.

So candidates — please keep an open mind. If full-time isn’t available right now, contract roles are a smart and practical option in today’s market.

Opening an Office in India? Start With the Operating Model, Not the Office  

Many global companies are now deciding how to build in India. The harder question is what the centre should become in five years, and the answer shapes everything from site to hiring. The context. India now hosts 2,117 global capability centres across 3,728 units, employing about 2.36 million people, and roughly 506 Forbes Global 2000 firms operate there. This is a mature ecosystem, so arriving late is not the risk. Arriving without a clear purpose is. The charter has shifted. Centres are moving from executing work for headquarters to owning products, platforms and strategic capabilities, and nearly half of those set up since FY2021 had AI as a core focus from inception. A centre designed as a cost line will struggle to become a capability. I would design it as the latter from day one. Four decisions, in order 
1. City and charter. Choose the location after the mandate. Karnataka alone hosts over 500 centres and around 35% of India’s GCC workforce, which means deep talent and fierce competition for it. 
2. Compliance by design. India’s data protection regime is being phased in. Operational obligations begin to bite from 13 November 2026, and full compliance is required by mid-May 2027. A new entrant should map data flows, consent and vendor contracts before go-live, not after. 
3. Talent before square feet. Leadership hires, the first fifty engineers and the career paths define the culture. Real estate is the easiest part to fix later. 
4. Ownership, not outsourcing. Give the centre a business outcome, such as a product line or a platform. Teams that own outcomes retain people and generate ideas. Where program leadership matters most. None of these decisions are technical. They are dependencies. 

Compliance affects architecture, architecture affects hiring, and hiring affects the timeline. Someone has to hold that map. This is where a program leader earns their seat: seeing the sequence early, naming the trade-offs calmly, and protecting the charter when pressure rises to cut corners. A closing thought. Climate disruption, data sovereignty, and geopolitics are not separate risks for a new entrant. They are one risk landscape. Organizations that build resilience into the first design will spend less time correcting courses later. #GCC

🏗️ In construction recruitment, the right person is about more than what’s written on their CV.

After watching the discussion around AI and recruitment on 60 Minutes last night, it got me thinking about how we identify the right people for construction roles.

In an industry where the wrong hire can impact project timelines, budgets, team morale and client relationships, how much could we miss by relying too heavily on keywords and automated screening?

A Site Manager might have all the right tickets and experience on paper, but how do they lead a team when a project falls behind schedule?

A Contract Administrator might tick every box technically, but how do they handle pressure, negotiate with subcontractors and build strong working relationships?

And an experienced candidate who hasn't worked on exactly the same type of project might bring transferable skills that make them an excellent fit.

These are things a CV alone cant always tell you.

✅ Technical skills and experience matter.
✅ Attitude, communication and leadership matter.
✅ Understanding a persons motivations, potential and suitability for a team matters.

AI can absolutely help streamline recruitment, but it shouldn't replace the conversations and judgement needed to understand what someone can really bring to a business.

For me, construction recruitment is about looking beyond the job title, the keywords and the CV to understand the person behind them.

Because the best candidate isn't always the one who looks perfect on paper. 

Its the one who can genuinely make a difference to your business.

At Frontline Construction Recruitment, I believe people-first recruitment means taking the time to get that match right.

💬 For those working in construction, would you trust an algorithm to shortlist your next Site Manager or Project Manager, or would you want a person involved in that decision?

If I were an SDR in 2026, I’d treat the role very differently.

If I were starting again, this is what I’d do.

[1] I’d sit in on calls after the meeting I booked. 

Not just discovery. I’d listen to demos, follow-ups, closed-won calls, closed-lost calls.

[2] I’d keep my own “why now” library.

Every time someone agrees to a meeting, I’d note what was happening in the account.
New leader? Expansion? Hiring? A broken process? Pressure from management? A contract coming up for renewal?

[3] I’d learn the money behind the problem.

If I’m selling something that saves time, I’d want to know how much time. 
If it reduces risk, what happens when that risk materialises?
If it improves revenue, where does that revenue leak today?

[4] I’d pick 20 accounts and know them unusually well.

A small set where I know the business, the people, what changed recently, who probably owns the problem, and who else might influence the decision.

[5] I’d use AI aggressively.

Research summaries. Notes. First drafts. CRM updates. Call prep.

But I’d be careful about what I do with the time it saves.

If I get an hour back and use it to send 40 more average emails, I haven’t gained much.
I’d use some of that hour to review a call, understand an account better, or prepare one genuinely good conversation.

If I were an SDR today, I’d try to become the person who understands why this account, why this person, why now, and what happens after they say yes.

About the Role

Are you a Computerized System Validation (CSV) expert with deep knowledge of GxP compliance, Agile delivery, and modern AI/ML validation frameworks?

We are looking for a Pharma Validation Subject Matter Expert (SME) to drive validation strategies, quality compliance, and lifecycle governance across regulated digital solutions and cutting-edge AI/ML models.Key Responsibilities • 

 Validation Strategy amp; Planning: Develop risk-based validation plans, testing approaches, CRS reviews, and ERES assessments across SDLC amp; Agile (ADLC) frameworks. • Requirements amp; Risk Management: Lead risk assessments, maintain strict traceability matrices (RTM), and ensure GxP and business requirements are fully addressed. 
  
Protocol Design amp; Test Execution: Author and execute IQ/OQ/PQ verification protocols, test scripts, and data migration strategies while managing defects and deviations. 

Regulatory Compliance amp; Quality Oversight: Maintain a constant state of validation readiness conforming to FDA 21 CFR Part 11, EU Annex 11, GAMP 5 (Second Edition), and GxP standards. 

AI/ML Validation Governance: Lead validation for non-deterministic models—covering AI risk assessments, bias testing, explainability, performance monitoring, and model drift governance.

 Cross-Functional Leadership: Partner with Data Scientists, Product Owners, Business SMEs, and Quality teams to evaluate change controls and deployment readiness. 

Required Qualifications • 🎓

 Education: Bachelor’s or Master’s in Life Sciences, Engineering, Computer Science, Information Systems, or Quality Assurance. 

 Experience: 5+ years in Computerized System Validation (CSV), Quality Assurance, or regulated system implementation within Pharma/Biotech. 

Core Expertise: Deep knowledge of GxP, FDA 21 CFR Part 11, GAMP 5, risk-based validation methodologies (FMEA), and Agile/SDLC processes. 

 Track Record: Hands-on experience with validation deliverables, traceability matrices, deviation write-ups, and regulatory audit support.
